passages.t: Isaac sends Jacob away, with a blessing
passages.happening:
Isaac calls Jacob and blesses him. “Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women,” he says (verse 1). Jacob is to go to Paddan-aram, to the house of Rebekah's father Bethuel, and marry one of the daughters of Laban, his mother's brother (verse 2).

Then Isaac blesses him again: “May God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, so that you may become a company of peoples” (verse 3). “And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants, so that you may possess the land where you dwell as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham” (verse 4).

So Isaac sends Jacob to Laban (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
This is the second time Isaac blesses Jacob. The first time he was tricked. This time he knows exactly whom he is blessing, and he does it in plain daylight. The father who wanted to bless Esau now passes on ‘the blessing of Abraham’ to Jacob on purpose.

Paddan-aram is the country around Haran, in the north, where Abraham's brother Nahor's family had settled. It lay hundreds of miles from Beersheba. Rebekah came from there (25:20).

Families like Abraham's preferred to marry within their own wider family. Abraham sent his servant there to find a wife for Isaac (chapter 24). Now Isaac sends Jacob himself. But Jacob goes with no camels, no gifts and no servants. Later he says he crossed the Jordan with only his staff (32:10). He goes as a man running for his life.

‘God Almighty’ translates El Shaddai, the name God used when he made his covenant with Abraham (17:1). Its exact meaning is uncertain. Isaac uses it here to pass that covenant on.

Notice the words ‘the land where you dwell as a foreigner’. Jacob is promised the land on the very day he leaves it.
passages.later:
God himself will repeat this blessing to Jacob years later at Bethel, using the same name: “I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 35:11).

Hebrews says the patriarchs lived in the land of promise “as a stranger in a foreign country” (Hebrews 11:9). The land promise is set out in the note on Genesis 12:4-9, with the ways Christians read it.
passages.asks: Isaac blessed Jacob a second time, this time knowing what he was doing. Ask whether there is a blessing you have withheld, or given grudgingly, that you could now give freely.

passages.t: Esau tries to please his father
passages.happening:
Esau learns that Isaac has blessed Jacob and sent him to find a wife, with the words, “Do not marry a Canaanite woman” (verse 6). He sees that Jacob has obeyed his father and mother (verse 7).

“And seeing that his father Isaac disapproved of the Canaanite women” (verse 8), Esau goes to Ishmael. He marries Mahalath, the daughter of Abraham's son Ishmael, “in addition to the wives he already had” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This short scene is sad. Esau has just lost the blessing. Now he notices, late, what his parents wanted, and he tries to win back his father's approval.

He marries into Abraham's family, through Ishmael, the son who was sent away. Mahalath is Esau's cousin. But he keeps the wives he already has. He adds a wife instead of changing anything.

The writer adds no comment. Esau is not mocked. He is a son trying, too late and in the wrong way, to be the son his father wanted.

The line of Ishmael and the line of Esau, the two sons not chosen to carry the promise, are joined by this marriage. Genesis gives each of them their own family list (25:12-18 and chapter 36).
passages.later:
Esau's family is listed in Genesis 36. There a wife of his is called Basemath, “daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth” (Genesis 36:3). Many readers take her to be Mahalath under another name. The lists of Esau's wives do not match exactly, and no one is sure why. Genesis gives the line not chosen its own account, with respect.

Hebrews names Esau among those who lost what they could not get back (Hebrews 12:16-17). The note on Genesis 27:30-40 explains how that passage is read.
passages.asks: Esau tried to win his father's approval with the right kind of marriage, too late. Ask whether you are still trying to earn the approval of someone whose blessing you missed. Then ask what it would mean to know that God's welcome is not earned that way.

passages.t: A stairway, and ‘I am with you’
passages.happening:
Jacob leaves Beersheba for Haran (verse 10). At sunset he stops at “a certain place”. He takes a stone, puts it under his head and lies down to sleep (verse 11).

“And Jacob had a dream about a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven, and God’s angels were going up and down the ladder” (verse 12).

The LORD stands at the top. “I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. I will give you and your descendants the land on which you now lie” (verse 13). His descendants will be “like the dust of the earth”, spreading west and east and north and south. “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your offspring” (verse 14).

“Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Picture Jacob. He is alone. He has lied to his father and robbed his brother. His brother wants him dead. He has left everything he knows, and he is sleeping on the ground with a stone for a pillow. He is not looking for God. He is running.

And this is where God speaks to him for the first time.

The BSB says ‘ladder’, but the Hebrew word, sullam, appears only here in the whole Bible, so its meaning has to be worked out. Many scholars link it with a word in Akkadian, the language of Babylon, that means a stairway or ramp. Others doubt that link. The old Greek translation used a word that can mean a ladder or a staircase. So many readers picture a great stairway or ramp, wide enough for angels to go up and down, rather than a narrow ladder.

Some scholars compare it with the stepped temple towers of Mesopotamia, called ziggurats, which had stairs or ramps up their sides and a shrine at the top. Others think that comparison goes further than the text does. Either way, readers have long heard an echo of Babel in chapter 11. There people built a tower up to heaven to make a name for themselves, and the city's name was understood in its own language as ‘the gate of the god’. Here no one builds anything. Heaven comes down to a man asleep on the ground, and he will call the place ‘the gate of heaven’.

Notice what God does not say. He does not scold Jacob for what he did to Esau. He does not lay down terms. He gives promises: the land, a family like the dust, blessing for all families of the earth, and above all, himself. ‘I am with you ... I will not leave you.’
passages.later:
Jesus takes up this dream when he meets Nathanael. He calls Nathanael “a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47), a sharp contrast with Jacob the deceiver, who will be renamed Israel. Then he says, “you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51). Jesus puts himself where the stairway stood. He is the place where heaven and earth meet.

The promise ‘I am with you’ runs through the Bible. Jesus' last words in Matthew are “surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Hebrews quotes God's promise, “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). A psalm asks, “Where can I flee from Your presence?” (Psalm 139:7).
passages.asks: God met Jacob at his lowest, on the run, without asking him to fix himself first. Ask whether you think God only meets people who have their lives in order. Then hear the words ‘I am with you’ as spoken to you, in the place where you are.

passages.t: ‘Surely the LORD is in this place’
passages.happening:
Jacob wakes up. “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it” (verse 16).

“And he was afraid and said, ‘How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God; this is the gate of heaven!’” (verse 17).

Early the next morning he takes the stone he slept on and sets it up as a pillar. He pours oil on top of it (verse 18). He names the place Bethel, though the city was first called Luz (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
‘I was unaware of it.’ Jacob had stopped at an ordinary place, wherever the sun happened to set. Now he learns God was there all along. Many readers find in this verse a picture of how God is often met: not where we planned, but where we stopped.

He is afraid. This is not terror at danger. It is awe, the fear of standing close to something far greater than you.

Bethel means ‘house of God’. The word ‘place’ comes up again and again in this passage. What began as ‘a certain place’ has become the house of God and the gate of heaven.

Jacob sets up the stone as a pillar, a standing stone to mark the spot. Pouring oil on it set it apart as holy. People in the ancient world marked places where they believed heaven and earth touched. Israel's law later forbade sacred pillars, because they were used in the worship of other gods (Deuteronomy 16:22). Here the stone is a marker of where God spoke, not something Jacob worships.

Bethel lay on the road through the hill country north of Jerusalem. Abraham had built an altar near it (12:8). It later had a sad history, as the next part says.
passages.later:
When the kingdom split, King Jeroboam set up a golden calf at Bethel: “One calf he set up in Bethel, and the other in Dan” (1 Kings 12:29). Amos warned, “Do not seek Bethel” (Amos 5:5), and Hosea called it Beth-aven, ‘house of wickedness’ (Hosea 4:15). The house of God became a house of false worship.

Hosea also remembers this night: “he found Him at Bethel and spoke with Him there” (Hosea 12:4).

Jacob will come back here years later, at God's word, to build an altar “to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau” (Genesis 35:1).
passages.asks: Jacob said, ‘The LORD is in this place, and I did not know it.’ Ask where you are right now that feels ordinary or hard. Then ask whether God might be there, and you have not noticed.

passages.happening:
Jacob makes a vow: “If God will be with me and watch over me on this journey, and if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear, so that I may return safely to my father’s house, then the LORD will be my God” (verses 20-21).

“And this stone I have set up as a pillar will be God’s house, and of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
A vow is a solemn promise made to God. In Israel a vow was often made in a time of need, and it was often conditional: ‘If you do this, I will do that.’ Hannah makes one when she prays for a son (1 Samuel 1:11).

Jacob's conditions are the same things God has just promised him: to be with him, to watch over him, to bring him back. He adds food and clothes. He is going into the unknown with almost nothing.

A tenth, or tithe, is what Abram gave Melchizedek (14:20). The note on Genesis 14:17-20 sets out how Christians read the tithe today, as a lasting pattern or as one example of generous giving. These notes do not settle it there either.

Notice what Jacob does not yet say. Earlier he called the LORD ‘your God’ to his father (27:20). Here he says that if God keeps his word, ‘the LORD will be my God’. He is not there yet. The rest of his story is the long road to that.
passages.later:
God reminds Jacob of this vow twenty years later: “I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the pillar and made a solemn vow to Me” (Genesis 31:13). Jacob keeps it when he returns and builds an altar there (Genesis 35:7).

Paul writes of giving: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
passages.hard:
Is Jacob's vow an act of faith, or is he bargaining with God? Readers answer in different ways.

Many hear the old Jacob in it. This is the man who bought a birthright for a bowl of stew. Now he sets terms with God: if you do this, then you will be my God. On this reading the chapter is honest about how little Jacob has changed overnight. God's promise came with no conditions, and Jacob answers with a contract.

Others point out that conditional vows were the normal way to make a vow in Israel. Hannah's vow is made the same way, and no one calls her a bargainer. Jacob's conditions simply repeat what God has just promised. To ask God to do what he said is not unbelief. Some scholars also note that the Hebrew can be read so that ‘then the LORD will be my God’ is part of the condition, not the promise.

The text does not settle Jacob's motives. It records the vow, and then it shows God keeping his side long before Jacob keeps his.
passages.asks: Jacob tried to set terms with God, and God kept his promises anyway. Ask whether you have made God a deal: if you do this, I will trust you. Then ask what it would look like to trust the God who has already promised to be with you.
